excerpt: A set is just a tidy collection with a rule. Here is how I teach the ICSE Class 6 Sets chapter, from the belongs-to symbol to subsets, with two real-life case studies your child can solve.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Tip a child’s school bag onto the floor and something interesting happens: they start sorting. Pens in one pile, notebooks in another, the half-eaten biscuit somewhere by itself. That instinct to group things by a clear rule is exactly what class 6 maths sets is about. A set is nothing more than a well-defined collection of objects — and ‘well-defined’ is the word that does all the heavy lifting. The set of vowels in English is fine. The set of ‘nice’ students is not, because nobody can agree who belongs.

In the ICSE Class 6 Sets chapter the ideas come fast but they are not hard, provided you keep tying each one back to a pile of real objects. Below I walk through the whole chapter the way I teach it, then solve two case studies of the kind your child will meet in the exam.

What a set is, and what ‘belongs to’ means

The objects inside a set are called its elements (or members). We name a set with a capital letter and hold its elements inside curly braces. So the set of the first three natural numbers is A = {1, 2, 3}. Each of 1, 2 and 3 is an element of A.

To say an element sits inside a set we use the symbol ∈, read as ‘belongs to’. So 2 ∈ A. To say something is not in the set we write ∉: here 7 ∉ A. That is the entire notation, and once a child reads ∈ out loud as ‘belongs to’ every time, the symbol stops being scary.

Roster form vs set-builder form

There are two ways to write the same set, and the exam expects both.

  • Roster (or tabular) form lists every element inside braces, separated by commas: V = {a, e, i, o, u}. Order does not matter and you never repeat an element.
  • Set-builder form states the rule instead of the list: V = {x : x is a vowel in the English alphabet}. Read the colon as ‘such that’.

When the list is short, roster form is quicker. When the list is long or endless — say, all even numbers — set-builder form is the sensible choice. A common slip I see: students repeat a letter when writing the set of letters in ‘MATHS’ versus ‘LETTER’. The set of letters in LETTER is {L, E, T, R}, not six items. Elements are counted once, full stop.

The types of sets you must know

Most of the chapter’s marks hide in naming sets correctly. Here is the full list in one place.

Type of setWhat it meansExample
Finite setYou can count the elements and stop{1, 2, 3, 4}
Infinite setThe elements never endThe set of natural numbers
Empty / null setHas no element at all; written ∅ or { }Months with 32 days
Singleton setHas exactly one elementThe set of even prime numbers = {2}
Equal setsSame elements, order ignored{1, 2, 3} = {3, 2, 1}
SubsetEvery element also sits in a bigger set{1, 2} is a subset of {1, 2, 3}

Two of these trip children up. The empty set feels like a trick — a set with nothing in it — but it is real and it has a symbol, ∅. And a singleton catches students out because {0} is a singleton with one element, while ∅ has none. Zero is a thing; nothing is not.

A quick word on subsets

If every element of set S is also in set T, then S is a subset of T, written S ⊆ T. The counter-intuitive bit worth remembering: the empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself. You do not need proofs in Class 6 — just the fact.

Case study 1: sorting the sports club

Read the passage, then solve. In 6-B, the games teacher lists the club members. Chess club C = {Aarav, Diya, Rohan}. Carrom club K = {Diya, Meera}. She wants to record this using sets.

  • Is C a finite set? Yes — you can count three members and stop, so C is finite.
  • Is Meera ∈ C? No. Meera belongs to K, not C, so Meera ∉ C.
  • Write, in roster form, the set of children who are in both clubs. Only Diya appears in both lists, so the answer is {Diya} — a singleton set.

Case study 2: the library shelf

A school library has this rule for one shelf: it holds only Maths textbooks for Class 6. On a certain Monday the shelf is completely empty because every copy is issued.

  • Is ‘the set of interesting books’ well-defined? No. ‘Interesting’ is an opinion, so it cannot form a set.
  • What kind of set describes the empty shelf on Monday? An empty (null) set, written ∅, because it has no element right now.
  • Write the shelf’s rule in set-builder form. B = {x : x is a Class 6 Maths textbook}. That is the rule the shelf follows even when it happens to be empty.

Notice how each question maps onto one idea from the chapter — well-defined collections, the null set, set-builder form. That is exactly how a good case study is built, and why practising a stack of them is worth more than re-reading the theory.

Try the quiz, then the case-study practice

The eight questions below cover the belongs-to symbol, roster and set-builder form, and every type of set from this chapter. Let your child answer first, then read the explanations together. quiz.title: Class 6 Maths Sets Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on elements, roster and set-builder form, and types of sets. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 6 Sets — elements, notation and types

questions.q: Which of the following is a well-defined set?
options: The collection of tall boys in a class
The collection of vowels in the English alphabet
questions.explanation: A set must be well-defined. ‘Tall’, ‘good’ and ‘interesting’ are opinions, but everyone agrees on the vowels a, e, i, o, u.

questions.q: The set of vowels written in roster form is:
questions.explanation: Roster form lists every element inside braces, so V = {a, e, i, o, u}.
∈ means ‘belongs to’. For A = {1, 2, 3}, we write 2 ∈ A.

questions.q: Which of these is an empty (null) set?
options: The set of natural numbers less than 1
The set of days in a week
questions.explanation: Natural numbers start at 1, so there are none less than 1. The set is empty, written ∅.

questions.q: Which set is a singleton set?
options: The set of even prime numbers
questions.explanation: The only even prime number is 2, so the set is {2} — exactly one element, a singleton.

questions.q: The set of natural numbers is:
questions.explanation: The natural numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, ... never end, so the set is infinite.

questions.q: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 2, 1}, then A and B are:
options: Not equal because the order differs
Equal sets, because order does not matter
questions.explanation: Two sets are equal when they have the same elements. Order is ignored, so A = B.

questions.q: S is the set of students who play chess and C is the set of all students in the class. Then S is:
questions.explanation: Every chess player is also a student in the class, so every element of S is in C. That makes S a subset of C, written S ⊆ C.

faq.q: What is a set in Class 6 maths?
faq.a: A set is a well-defined collection of objects, called its elements. ‘Well-defined’ means anyone can decide for certain whether an object belongs. The vowels {a, e, i, o, u} form a set; ‘nice students’ do not, because that is a matter of opinion.

faq.q: What is the difference between roster form and set-builder form?
faq.a: Roster form lists every element inside braces, like V = {a, e, i, o, u}. Set-builder form states the rule instead, like V = {x : x is a vowel}. Use roster form for short lists and set-builder form when the list is long or endless.
It means ‘belongs to’. If A = {1, 2, 3}, then 2 ∈ A shows that 2 is an element of A. To say something is not in the set, we use ∉, so 7 ∉ A.

faq.q: What is the difference between an empty set and a singleton set?
faq.a: An empty (null) set has no elements at all and is written ∅ or { }. A singleton set has exactly one element, such as {0} or the set of even prime numbers {2}. Zero counts as an element, so {0} is a singleton, not empty.
